Rendering performance

plotly (CRAN) vs. plot_ly() on plotly.core vs. go_figure() with float32 vs. plotly.py

Source: vignettes/render-performance.qmd

plotly.core makes large figures much quicker to build, save, load and draw than the CRAN plotly release, and lighter on browser memory, for plot_ly() code unchanged and even more so for go_figure() with as_float32(). This vignette shows the results first, then how the gains were made; the numbers and how the benchmarks are run are in the appendix.

Variant Code Data sent to the browser as
release plot_ly() with the CRAN plotly release JSON numbers / date strings
core_backend the same plot_ly() code with the development plotly, which renders with plotly.core base64 typed arrays (float64)
go_figure_f32 go_figure() and add_*() with as_float32(), saved with write_html() base64 typed arrays (float32)
plotly_py plotly.py go.Figure() with numpy float64 base64 typed arrays (float64), ISO date strings
plotly_py_f32 plotly.py go.Figure() with numpy float32 base64 typed arrays (float32), ISO date strings

Results

Each chart shows one measurement for the three cases, against the number of values plotted (both axes on log scales), medians over 3 runs (2026-11-16, Apple M3 Pro, Chrome/157.0.8103.78). Lower is better throughout. The numbers are in the results tables.

Show the chart code
# one panel per case; x: values plotted, y: the measurement
metric_chart <- function(col, label) {
  d <- res[order(res$variant, res$case, res$values), c("variant", "case", "values", col)]
  names(d)[4] <- "value"
  fig <- px_line(
    d, x = "values", y = "value", color = "variant", facet_col = "case",
    markers = TRUE, log_x = TRUE, log_y = TRUE,
    category_orders = list(variant = variants, case = levels(res$case)),
    # R in blues, Python in oranges; the darkest of each is the float32 variant
    color_discrete_map = list(release = "#6baed6", core_backend = "#2171b5", go_figure_f32 = "#08306b",
                              plotly_py = "#fd8d3c", plotly_py_f32 = "#a63603"),
    labels = list(values = "values plotted", value = label, variant = ""),
    template = "plotly_white"
  )
  # each panel its own y range: the cases differ in scale
  for (ax in grep("^yaxis", names(fig$layout), value = TRUE)) {
    fig$layout[[ax]]$matches <- NULL
    fig$layout[[ax]]$showticklabels <- TRUE
  }
  for (ax in grep("^xaxis", names(fig$layout), value = TRUE)) fig$layout[[ax]]$dtick <- 1
  fig |>
    for_each_annotation(function(a) {
      a$text <- sub("^[^=]*=", "", a$text) # "case=heatmap" -> "heatmap"
      a
    }) |>
    update_layout(legend = list(orientation = "h", y = 1.12, yanchor = "bottom", x = 0)) |>
    partial_bundle("auto")
}

Build + write time

Show the chart code
metric_chart("build_sec", "build + write (s)")

This is the wait in R before anything can be shown: in the console or RStudio, while knitting a report, or on every re-render in a Shiny app. For the 2000 × 2000 heatmap, CRAN plotly keeps R busy for 12.7 s; the same plot_ly() code with plotly.core takes 0.8 s, and go_figure() with as_float32() 0.10 s, faster than plotly.py.

Page size

Show the chart code
metric_chart("html_mb", "HTML (MB)")

The size of the saved page or the data a Shiny app sends: it’s what a viewer on a remote server or slow connection waits to download, and what makes self-contained reports too big to email or attach. The 1M-point time series goes from 96 MB with CRAN plotly to 21 MB, and 10 series sharing x from 67 MB to 6.4 MB, since x is sent once.

Load time

Show the chart code
metric_chart("load_sec", "load (s)")

The time from opening the page to the plot appearing, here with no network in between. A heatmap that CRAN plotly takes 8.4 s to show appears in 2.2 s with plotly.core (1.5 s with float32). For small figures (under about 100,000 values) CRAN plotly loads slightly faster, because plotly.js 4 is a larger script; see partial_bundle().

Drawing time (newPlot)

Show the chart code
metric_chart("newplot_sec", "newPlot (s)")

The part of the load plotly.js spends drawing, about the same for every variant (0.77 s and 0.67 s for the heatmap). The gains come from getting data to plotly.js faster, not from plotly.js drawing faster, so zooming and other redraws after load feel the same.

Peak browser memory

Show the chart code
metric_chart("peak_renderer_mb", "peak renderer (MB)")

The most memory the page’s browser process uses while loading; when a tab exceeds what the browser or machine allows, it crashes (“Aw, Snap!” in Chrome), which is most likely on laptops with little memory, on phones, or with several large plots on one page. The heatmap peaks at 1039 MB with CRAN plotly and 590 MB with go_figure() and float32.

Memory held after load

Show the chart code
metric_chart("js_heap_mb", "JS heap after load (MB)")

The JavaScript memory the plot keeps while it stays open, which adds up on dashboards and reports with many plots. For the 1M-point time series it falls from 291 MB with CRAN plotly to 205 MB with plotly.core and 187 MB with float32.

How the gains were made

Numbers here are medians from the results, at the largest size of each case, unless marked as a standalone timing (measured separately, during development).

How plotly.core sends data to the browser

Numeric arrays as base64 typed arrays. Numeric vectors and matrices in traces are sent as {dtype, bdata, shape}, as plotly.py does, rather than as JSON numbers; whole numbers are narrowed to the smallest integer type without loss. A double takes 10.7 bytes of base64 instead of about 18–20 characters of JSON, and the browser decodes the bytes straight into a typed array instead of parsing text. For the heatmap this takes the page from 164.4 MB (CRAN plotly) to 42.7 MB (plot_ly() with plotly.core), the load time from 8.39 s to 2.20 s, and the renderer’s peak memory from 1039 MB to 650 MB. plotly.js’s own newPlot() time is about the same for every variant, so the faster loads come from fetching, parsing and decoding less data, not from plotly.js itself.

Date-times as numbers. Dates and date-times are sent as typed arrays of days or milliseconds; the widget’s JavaScript turns them back into the strings R would have written. UTC offsets are looked up once per 15-minute bin rather than once per value. For the 1M-point time series, CRAN plotly writes a page of 95.9 MB in 7.63 s; with plotly.core the same plot_ly() code writes 21.3 MB in 0.41 s. plotly.py writes date-times as text, so its time series pages are larger (43.3 MB).

Encoding in C. The typed arrays are encoded in C (src/typed_array.c): one pass to find the narrowest type, then base64 written straight into one buffer, as data.table’s fwrite() writes its output. jsonlite writes the rest of the figure with placeholders and C copies the encoded arrays in, so the large strings never pass through R. For the 2000 × 2000 float32 heatmap the whole JSON step takes about 0.06 s (standalone timing).

Arrays repeated in a figure are sent once. An array used by several traces, like the x of the 10 time series, is encoded once and referenced after that; in the browser every trace uses the same object, and date strings are restored once. With 10 series of 100,000 points, plot_ly() with plotly.core writes 11.7 MB and go_figure() 6.4 MB, against 67.4 MB for CRAN plotly and 43.3 MB for plotly.py, which repeat x in each trace. Those pages are smaller than the single 1M-point series and load faster (1.00 s against 1.28 s for go_figure()).

as_float32(). Doubles marked with as_float32() are sent in single precision, 4 bytes instead of 8 (about 7 significant digits, which is what WebGL draws with). It halves the heatmap’s page (42.7 to 21.3 MB) and cuts the JavaScript memory left after loading (153 to 115 MB) and the load time (2.20 to 1.49 s). For the time series only y is halved; x stays in double precision.

write_html(). htmlwidgets lays out the page and the figure’s data is then written to the file directly, rather than passed through htmltools as one long string, which is searched and copied several times. This is most of the difference between go_figure() and plot_ly() in build + write time: 0.103 s for the heatmap (0.133 s for plotly.py with float32), and 0.080 s for the 1M-point time series (0.475 s). write_html() also takes plot_ly() figures: saving the plot_ly() heatmap takes about 0.2 s with it instead of about 0.8 s with saveWidget() (standalone timing).

Building plot_ly() figures in plotly

A faster plotly_build(). The development plotly computes each group’s rows once rather than once per column, sorts with radix order() only when rows are out of order, and replaces the dplyr, tibble, rlang, tidyr and purrr calls in the build with base R. That’s about twice as fast on large plots (three 1M-point WebGL traces: 0.70 s to 0.30 s, standalone timing).

Heatmaps. Checking whether a heatmap’s z holds a single colour value used unique() on its rows; it now uses rowSums(). plotly_build() of the 2000 × 2000 heatmap takes 0.04 s instead of 0.15 s (standalone timing). Most of the plot_ly() heatmap’s remaining 0.79 s is htmlwidgets::saveWidget() handling the large page, which write_html() avoids.

What doesn’t help (yet)

  • Partial bundles. partial_bundle() loads a smaller plotly.js with only the trace types a figure uses, but every variant here loads the full bundle.
  • A larger plotly.js. plotly.js 4 is larger to load than the 2.x CRAN plotly bundles, so for small figures (under about 100,000 values) CRAN plotly loads faster; the data dominates above that.
  • plotly.js 4 itself draws in about the same time as plotly.js 2 (newPlot above).

Notes

  • The variants use different plotly.js versions (see above), so newPlot times include plotly.js differences as well as the data format; plotly.js 4 is also larger to load (all variants load a full bundle). “JS transferred (MB)” is all JavaScript the page fetched (plotly.js, htmlwidgets, bindings) as sent by the server, which compresses it.
  • Load times are from localhost: on a real network, the HTML size adds transfer time.
  • Chrome runs headless on the machine’s GPU where it has one (WebGL via ANGLE), so WebGL drawing reflects the hardware.
  • float32 keeps about 7 significant digits (see ?as_float32). Date-times are unaffected: plotly.core sends them as float64 milliseconds; plotly.py and the release send ISO strings.
  • Renderer memory is resident set size as the OS reports it, sampled every 20 ms, so short spikes can be missed; the GPU process’s memory (WebGL buffers) is not included.

Running the benchmarks

The benchmarks take several minutes and need software outside R (headless Chrome via chromote, and Python with plotly, numpy and pandas), so building this vignette shows results saved from an earlier run, read from the render-performance/ folder next to it. To rerun them, render this file with the environment variable PLOTLY_CORE_RUN_BENCHMARKS=true; the code below then runs before the results are shown, and new results are saved to render-performance/:

PLOTLY_CORE_RUN_BENCHMARKS=true quarto render vignettes/render-performance.qmd \
  -P python:/path/to/python -P release_lib:/path/to/lib-with-cran-plotly

Parameters (-P name:value): python, a Python with plotly, numpy and pandas; release_lib, a library with the CRAN plotly (installed there if missing); core_lib, a library with the development plotly and plotly.core (default: the first of .libPaths()); ts_sizes, ms_sizes, hm_sizes and reps.

What is measured

Three use cases, over a range of sizes:

  • Large time series: one scattergl line trace with date-time x (1 s steps) and a random walk y.
  • 10 time series: ten scattergl line traces, one per column of a wide data frame, sharing the same date-time x. plotly.core sends an array repeated in a figure once (see widget_to_JSON()), so x is sent once rather than ten times.
  • Large matrix heatmap: one heatmap trace of an n × n matrix.

Metrics:

  • Build + write (s): R or Python time from the figure-making call to the standalone HTML page written to disk (htmlwidgets::saveWidget() for plot_ly(), write_html() for go_figure(), fig.write_html() in Python), after one untimed warm-up run, in a fresh process per variant.
  • HTML (MB): the size of the page, which holds the figure data (plotly.js is a separate file).
  • Load time (s): in headless Chrome, from navigation start to the first frame painted after plotly.js’s newPlot() resolves. Pages are served over HTTP from localhost with the browser cache disabled, so the time covers fetching and parsing plotly.js and the page, decoding the data and plotting, but no network latency.
  • newPlot (s): the time plotly.js itself spends in newPlot(), part of the load time.
  • Peak renderer memory (MB): the largest resident memory of the page’s renderer process while loading, sampled every 20 ms.
  • JS heap after load (MB): JavaScript heap in use after load and a forced garbage collection, plus array buffers (where Chrome reports them).

Libraries 

dir.create(file.path(wd, "data"), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create(pages_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create(results_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

release_lib <- if (nzchar(params$release_lib)) params$release_lib else file.path(wd, "lib-release")
core_lib <- if (nzchar(params$core_lib)) params$core_lib else .libPaths()[1]
if (!file.exists(file.path(release_lib, "plotly", "DESCRIPTION"))) {
  dir.create(release_lib, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
  install.packages("plotly", lib = release_lib, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org",
                   type = "source", dependencies = FALSE)
}
libs <- list(release = release_lib, core_backend = core_lib, go_figure_f32 = core_lib)
python <- params$python

Data

The data is generated once in R and written as little-endian doubles, so that every variant (R and Python) plots the same values.

cases <- rbind(
  data.frame(case = "timeseries", size = params$ts_sizes, values = params$ts_sizes),
  data.frame(case = "multiseries", size = params$ms_sizes, values = params$ms_sizes * 10),
  data.frame(case = "heatmap", size = params$hm_sizes, values = params$hm_sizes^2)
)
cases$file <- file.path(wd, "data", sprintf("%s-%d.bin", cases$case, cases$size))
set.seed(2024)
for (i in seq_len(nrow(cases))) {
  n <- cases$size[i]
  v <- if (cases$case[i] == "timeseries") {
    cumsum(rnorm(n))
  } else if (cases$case[i] == "multiseries") {
    as.vector(apply(matrix(rnorm(n * 10), n), 2, cumsum))
  } else {
    s <- seq(0, 6 * pi, length.out = n)
    as.vector(outer(sin(s), cos(s)) + rnorm(n * n, sd = 0.1))
  }
  writeBin(v, cases$file[i], endian = "little")
}

Figure code

The R code for each variant. Every function gets the time series as t (POSIXct, UTC) and y; the 10 series as a data frame d with columns t and y01, …, y10; or the heatmap as the matrix z.

figures <- list(
  release = list(
    timeseries = function(t, y) plot_ly(x = t, y = y, type = "scattergl", mode = "lines"),
    multiseries = function(d) {
      p <- plot_ly(d, x = ~t)
      for (col in names(d)[-1]) {
        p <- add_trace(p, y = d[[col]], name = col, type = "scattergl", mode = "lines")
      }
      p
    },
    heatmap = function(z) plot_ly(z = z, type = "heatmap")
  ),
  go_figure_f32 = list(
    timeseries = function(t, y) {
      go_figure() |> add_scattergl(x = t, y = as_float32(y), mode = "lines")
    },
    multiseries = function(d) {
      fig <- go_figure()
      for (col in names(d)[-1]) {
        fig <- add_scattergl(fig, x = d$t, y = as_float32(d[[col]]), name = col, mode = "lines")
      }
      fig
    },
    heatmap = function(z) go_figure() |> add_heatmap(z = as_float32(z))
  )
)
# the same plot_ly() code, run with the development plotly
figures$core_backend <- figures$release

# how each variant writes its page
writers <- list(
  release = function(p, file) htmlwidgets::saveWidget(p, file, selfcontained = FALSE, libdir = "lib"),
  core_backend = function(p, file) htmlwidgets::saveWidget(p, file, selfcontained = FALSE, libdir = "lib"),
  go_figure_f32 = function(fig, file) write_html(fig, file, selfcontained = FALSE, libdir = "lib")
)

The plotly.py equivalents (plotly_py_f32 converts the arrays with astype(np.float32) before timing starts, as as_float32() only marks them):

import gc, json, sys, time
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, plotly.graph_objects as go

variant, cases_file, reps, outdir = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2], int(sys.argv[3]), sys.argv[4]
f32 = variant == "plotly_py_f32"

def timeseries(t, y):
    return go.Figure(go.Scattergl(x=t, y=y, mode="lines"))

def multiseries(t, Y):
    fig = go.Figure()
    for j in range(Y.shape[1]):
        fig.add_trace(go.Scattergl(x=t, y=Y[:, j], name=f"y{j + 1:02d}", mode="lines"))
    return fig

def heatmap(z):
    return go.Figure(go.Heatmap(z=z))

out = []
for case in json.load(open(cases_file)):
    n, kind = case["size"], case["case"]
    v = np.fromfile(case["file"], dtype="<f8")
    if f32:
        v = v.astype(np.float32)
    if kind == "timeseries":
        args = (pd.date_range("2024-01-01", periods=n, freq="s"), v)
        make = timeseries
    elif kind == "multiseries":
        args = (pd.date_range("2024-01-01", periods=n, freq="s"), v.reshape((n, 10), order="F"))
        make = multiseries
    else:
        args = (v.reshape((n, n), order="F"),)
        make = heatmap
    page = f"{outdir}/{kind}-{n}.html"
    save = lambda: make(*args).write_html(page, include_plotlyjs="directory", full_html=True)
    save()  # warm-up; also the page the browser loads
    for rep in range(reps):
        gc.collect()
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        save()
        out.append(dict(variant=variant, case=kind, size=n, rep=rep + 1,
                        build_sec=time.perf_counter() - t0))
json.dump(out, sys.stdout)

Build + write timings

Each variant runs in its own fresh process: R variants with callr and the library holding the right plotly version first on the library path.

r_worker <- function(variant, fns, write, cases, reps, outdir) {
  suppressPackageStartupMessages(
    if (variant == "go_figure_f32") library(plotly.core) else library(plotly)
  )
  dir.create(outdir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
  out <- list()
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(cases))) {
    n <- cases$size[i]
    v <- readBin(cases$file[i], "double", n = cases$values[i], endian = "little")
    t <- as.POSIXct("2024-01-01", tz = "UTC") + seq_len(n) - 1
    if (cases$case[i] == "timeseries") {
      args <- list(t = t, y = v)
    } else if (cases$case[i] == "multiseries") {
      y <- matrix(v, n, 10, dimnames = list(NULL, sprintf("y%02d", 1:10)))
      args <- list(d = data.frame(t = t, y))
    } else {
      args <- list(z = matrix(v, n, n))
    }
    make <- fns[[cases$case[i]]]
    page <- file.path(outdir, sprintf("%s-%d.html", cases$case[i], n))
    save <- function() write(do.call(make, args), page)
    save() # warm-up; also the page the browser loads
    for (rep in seq_len(reps)) {
      gc()
      out[[length(out) + 1]] <- data.frame(
        variant = variant, case = cases$case[i], size = n, rep = rep,
        build_sec = system.time(save())[["elapsed"]]
      )
    }
  }
  do.call(rbind, out)
}

build_r <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(figures), function(v) {
  callr::r(r_worker, list(v, figures[[v]], writers[[v]], cases, reps, file.path(pages_dir, v)),
           libpath = c(libs[[v]], .libPaths()))
}))

Browser measurements

A script injected before any page script runs wraps plotly.js’s newPlot()/react()/plot() to time the first plot, and marks the first frame painted after it:

(function () {
  var B = window.__bench = { done: false };
  function finish() {
    if (B.end != null) return;
    B.end = performance.now();
    requestAnimationFrame(function () {
      setTimeout(function () { B.painted = performance.now(); B.done = true; }, 0);
    });
  }
  // plotly.js 3+ exports are read-only, so the wrapper is a new object
  // inheriting from Plotly, with timed newPlot()/react()/plot()
  function wrap(P) {
    if (!P || P.__benchWrapped) return P;
    var W = Object.create(P);
    ["newPlot", "react", "plot"].forEach(function (k) {
      var orig = P[k];
      if (typeof orig !== "function") return;
      W[k] = function () {
        if (B.start == null) B.start = performance.now();
        var r = orig.apply(P, arguments);
        Promise.resolve(r).then(finish, function (e) { B.error = String(e); B.done = true; });
        return r;
      };
    });
    W.__benchWrapped = true;
    return W;
  }
  var plotly;
  Object.defineProperty(window, "Plotly", {
    configurable: true,
    get: function () { return plotly; },
    set: function (v) { plotly = wrap(v); }
  });
  window.addEventListener("error", function (e) { B.error = String(e.message); B.done = true; });
})();
hook_js <- paste(readLines(file.path(wd, "hook.js")), collapse = "\n")
chrome <- chromote::Chromote$new()

# serve the pages over HTTP from localhost
port <- httpuv::randomPort()

                      list(pages_dir, port))
for (i in 1:50) {
  if (!inherits(try(suppressWarnings(readLines(sprintf("http://127.0.0.1:%d/", port), n = 1)),
                    silent = TRUE), "try-error")) break
  Sys.sleep(0.1)
}

# samples the largest renderer process's memory (RSS) every 20 ms until killed
sampler <- function(browser_pid, out) {
  peak <- 0
  writeLines("0", out) # started
  repeat {
    procs <- try(ps::ps_children(ps::ps_handle(browser_pid), recursive = TRUE), silent = TRUE)
    if (!inherits(procs, "try-error")) {
      for (p in procs) {
        rss <- try({
          if (any(grepl("--type=renderer", ps::ps_cmdline(p), fixed = TRUE))) ps::ps_memory_info(p)[["rss"]] else 0
        }, silent = TRUE)
        if (is.numeric(rss) && rss > peak) {
          peak <- rss
          writeLines(format(peak, scientific = FALSE), out)
        }
      }
    }
    Sys.sleep(0.02)
  }
}
browser_pid <- chrome$get_browser()$get_process()$get_pid()

measure_page <- function(url, timeout = 300) {
  s <- chromote::ChromoteSession$new(parent = chrome, width = 1000, height = 600)
  on.exit(s$close(), add = TRUE)
  s$Network$enable()
  s$Network$setCacheDisabled(cacheDisabled = TRUE)
  s$Page$enable() # needed for the injected script to run
  s$Page$addScriptToEvaluateOnNewDocument(source = hook_js)
  peak_file <- tempfile()
  smp <- callr::r_bg(sampler, list(browser_pid, peak_file))
  on.exit(smp$kill(), add = TRUE)
  # wait for the sampler to start
  for (i in 1:100) if (file.exists(peak_file)) break else Sys.sleep(0.05)
  Sys.sleep(0.1)
  s$Page$navigate(url, wait_ = FALSE) # large pages can take a while to commit
  t0 <- Sys.time()
  repeat {
    done <- s$Runtime$evaluate("!!(window.__bench && window.__bench.done)", timeout_ = timeout)$result$value
    if (isTRUE(done)) break
    if (difftime(Sys.time(), t0, units = "secs") > timeout) stop("timed out loading ", url)
    Sys.sleep(0.05)
  }
  Sys.sleep(0.3)
  smp$kill()
  b <- jsonlite::fromJSON(s$Runtime$evaluate(
    "JSON.stringify(Object.assign({}, window.__bench, {js_bytes: performance.getEntriesByType('resource')
       .filter(e => /\\.js$/.test(e.name)).reduce((a, e) => a + e.encodedBodySize, 0)}))"
  )$result$value)
  if (!is.null(b$error)) stop(url, ": ", b$error)
  s$HeapProfiler$collectGarbage()
  heap <- s$Runtime$getHeapUsage()
  data.frame(
    load_sec = b$painted / 1000,
    newplot_sec = (b$end - b$start) / 1000,
    js_mb = b$js_bytes / 1e6,
    peak_renderer_mb = as.numeric(readLines(peak_file, warn = FALSE)) / 1e6,
    js_heap_mb = (heap$usedSize + if (is.null(heap$backingStorageSize)) 0 else heap$backingStorageSize) / 1e6
  )
}

# on a failure (e.g. Chrome not responding), restart Chrome and try the page once more
measure_retry <- function(url) {
  tryCatch(measure_page(url), error = function(e) {
    message("retrying ", url, " after: ", conditionMessage(e))
    try(chrome$close(), silent = TRUE)
    chrome <<- chromote::Chromote$new()
    browser_pid <<- chrome$get_browser()$get_process()$get_pid()
    measure_page(url)
  })
}

set.seed(1)
browser <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(reps), function(rep) {
  # shuffle the page order each round, so drift doesn't favour a variant
  do.call(rbind, lapply(sample(nrow(pages)), function(i) {
    cbind(pages[i, c("variant", "case", "size")], rep = rep,
          measure_retry(sprintf("http://127.0.0.1:%d/%s", port, pages$path[i])))
  }))
}))
server$kill()

Environment

Results above are from a run on 2026-11-16 on macOS 26.5.1 (Apple M3 Pro), with R version 4.4.2 (2024-10-31) and Chrome/157.0.8103.78 (headless), and these versions:

variant plotly plotly.core plotly.js
release 4.12.1 2.25.2
core_backend, go_figure_f32 4.12.1.9000 0.1.0 4.3.0
plotly_py, plotly_py_f32 7.1.0 (Python; numpy 2.0.2, pandas 2.3.3) 4.1.1 
r_versions <- function(lib) {
  callr::r(function() {
    js_version <- function(pkg, file) {
      f <- system.file("htmlwidgets", "lib", "plotlyjs", file, package = pkg)
      if (!nzchar(f)) return(NA_character_)
      head <- readChar(f, 500)
      sub("^v", "", regmatches(head, regexpr("v[0-9]+\\.[0-9]+\\.[0-9]+", head)))
    }
    # the development plotly draws with plotly.core's plotly.js
    uses_core <- grepl("plotly.core", utils::packageDescription("plotly")$Imports, fixed = TRUE)
    data.frame(
      plotly = as.character(utils::packageVersion("plotly")),
      plotly.core = if (uses_core) as.character(utils::packageVersion("plotly.core")) else NA,
      plotly.js = if (uses_core) js_version("plotly.core", "plotly.min.js") else js_version("plotly", "plotly-latest.min.js")
    )
  }, libpath = c(lib, .libPaths()))
}

  "pandas=pandas.__version__, plotlyjs=o.get_plotlyjs_version())))"))), stdout = TRUE))
